argument: Avicenna broke from Aristotle's view that mind and body are inseparable, using the flying man thought experiment to argue that a person's self-awareness persists even when totally stripped of all bodily sensation, proving the mind and body are separate entities. This move, similar in spirit to Descartes's later 'I think, therefore I am,' let Avicenna argue for an immortal soul, though it put him at odds with orthodox Islamic belief in bodily resurrection.
keyIdeas: Aristotle held that mind (soul) and body are inseparable, like an iPhone's form and its materials -- melt the materials down and it's no longer an iPhone, and the soul likewise cannot outlast the body.
This creates a problem for an eternal afterlife: if soul and body are truly one, there's no reason to think the soul survives the body's destruction.

In the flying man thought experiment, a person created fully formed but with all sensation stripped away -- sight, touch, even awareness of their own limbs -- would still affirm their own existence, showing the self is not identical to the body.
The thought experiment therefore concludes that the human body and mind are separate from each other, not merely that self-awareness proves existence.

Avicenna's argument differs from Descartes's 'I think, therefore I am': Descartes's cogito only establishes that thought proves existence, while the flying man goes further to conclude mind and body are separable -- and the episode notes Saint Augustine's earlier refutation of skepticism may deserve credit as an even earlier version of this self-certainty argument.

terms.def: Avicenna's scenario of a person created in mid-air with no sensory input, used to show self-awareness persists without any bodily perception.
Aristotle's term for the mind's capacity to reason, which he held was inseparable from the body.
Descartes's later argument that the act of thinking alone proves one's own existence.
Avicenna's most famous work, in which he 'heals' or reconciles Aristotle's philosophy with Islamic theology.

The orthodox Islamic belief, as the episode puts it, that 'both body and mind are resurrected into the afterlife' -- a view Avicenna's flying man argument (implying a body-independent, immortal soul) put him at odds with.
